title: Effective theory of the hidden-order pseudogap phase in a doped antiferromagnet
authors: Gaia De Paciani, Gesa Dünnweber, Johannes Poersch, Simon M. Linsel, Henning Schlömer, Fabian Grusdt
abstract: The microscopic origin of the pseudogap phase constitutes a longstanding puzzle related to the emergence of high-temperature superconductivity in cuprate materials. In this work, we develop an effective model for doped antiferromagnets in terms of fluctuating stripes, or string-like domain walls, which obscure the antiferromagnetic order of the spin background. The open ends of such domain walls of the N'eel order are treated as vortices in the resulting lattice gauge theory. We numerically evaluate the phase diagram by classical Monte Carlo simulations, using percolation-based geometric order parameters to diagnose hidden N'eel order. At high temperatures, we identify a BKT-type crossover in which the domain wall ends become deconfined. We interpret this as the $T^*$ crossover from the hidden order regime to the paramagnetic metal above. At low temperatures, we identify stripe instabilities. Predictions of our effective model can be tested in ultracold fermion quantum simulators.
summary: This work develops an effective string model for doped antiferromagnets to explain the pseudogap phase. By treating fluctuating Néel order as domain walls with vortex ends, the authors map the pseudogap transition onto a topological BKT-type crossover. The findings suggest that the pseudogap is governed by the confinement of these string ends rather than simple symmetry breaking.
main_problem: The paper addresses the long-standing puzzle of the microscopic origin of the pseudogap phase in cuprate superconductors, linking it to magnetic fluctuations and doping.
main_result: The pseudogap boundary ($T^*$) is identified as a topological crossover associated with the confinement/deconfinement of vortex ends in the effective string model, rather than the onset of a local order parameter.
method: The authors developed an effective model based on fluctuating Néel domain walls (stripes) and analyzed its phase diagram using classical Monte Carlo simulations.
model_or_system: The system is a doped antiferromagnet modeled by an effective string theory where domain walls are treated as 1D strings. The Hamiltonian incorporates terms for the spin background and vortex interactions, leading to a lattice gauge theory description.
key_observables: Percolation-based geometric order parameters (POPs), the $U(1)$ correlation function decay (algebraic vs. exponential), and the compressibility (showing a Widom line).
important_parameters: Doping ($\delta$), temperature ($T$), and the ratio of correlation lengths ($\xi^* \gg d$).
main_assumptions: The effective model assumes the correlation length of the spin background ($\xi^*$) is much larger than the separation of the open string ends ($d$).
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the phase diagram, distinguishing between the spin-pseudogap regime and the hidden-order pseudogap phase via fluctuating stripes and vortex ends.
paper_structure: The paper develops the effective string model, analyzes the phase diagram using Monte Carlo simulations to detect percolation and BKT crossovers, and interprets these transitions in the context of the pseudogap physics.
why_interesting: The use of topological concepts (vortices, confinement/deconfinement) to describe a phase transition in a strongly correlated material is highly relevant to understanding emergent order in quantum many-body systems.

FIG. 4. Compressibility peak from the percolation transition. We show the behavior of the compressibility, cal- culated in the effective model using Eq (7), for different tem- peratures and effective hole-doping δ. In the low- T regime, where open strings are confined, a pronounced maximum of the compressibility (Widom line) is revealed around the perco- lation transition. For higher temperatures, where open strings deconfine, the maximum, becomes less pronounced while the compressibility flattens out and decreases.
